config.title: Type custom hook return tuples

intro.title: Type custom hook return tuples
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a custom React hook that returns a typed tuple, a specific array structure where each position has a fixed type. You will learn how to use TypeScript to explicitly define the return type of your hook, ensuring type safety for the values it provides. The core concept involves leveraging TypeScript's tuple types to enforce the order and types of multiple return values, such as a state variable and its setter function. You will work with React hooks like useState and apply TypeScript generics to create a reusable and well-typed custom hook. By the end, you'll understand how to type custom hooks to prevent errors and improve code clarity in your TypeScript projects.
intro.usecase: Custom hook return tuples are essential for building interactive UI components like search filters, data tables, and form controls in modern applications. For example, in an e-commerce dashboard, a `useProductFilter` hook might return `[filters, setFilters, resetFilters]` to manage filter states for product listings. This pattern provides clear, predictable APIs that developers can easily consume in components like filter panels or data grids. By typing these tuples properly, you ensure autocomplete support and prevent runtime errors when building complex features like multi-step forms or real-time data visualizations.

objectives: Construct a custom hook that returns a tuple of values and functions
Apply explicit tuple type annotations to a custom hook's return statement
Implement a custom hook that manages state and returns a typed tuple
Integrate a typed custom hook into a functional component
Manipulate tuple elements by destructuring the hook's return value
Configure a custom hook to return a tuple with optional elements
Update component logic using the typed values from a custom hook tuple

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package to use React components and state management.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The imports are added, enabling the use of React components and state in the file.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've imported React, but remember to also import useState from 'react' to manage state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are missing or incorrect. Ensure you import both React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Create a custom hook skeleton
steps.instruction: Create a function called useCounter that will serve as our custom hook. It should be a function declaration or arrow function that returns an empty tuple for now.
steps.hint: Define a function named useCounter. You can use either 'function useCounter()' or 'const useCounter = () =>'. Make sure it returns an empty array [] to represent a tuple.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';
// Create your useCounter hook here
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named useCounter is defined that returns an empty tuple.
successCriteria: The useCounter function is created and returns an empty array [].
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've defined a function called useCounter that returns an empty array [].
steps.feedbackWrong: Create a function named useCounter that returns an empty array [].

steps.title: Add state to the custom hook
steps.instruction: Inside your useCounter hook, declare a count state variable using useState with an initial value of 0.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier to create a state variable and its setter function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useCounter hook will have a count state variable initialized to 0.
successCriteria: useCounter contains a count state variable declared with useState(0).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added state to your custom hook.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState with an initial value of 0 inside the useCounter function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useCounter hook should contain a count state variable declared with useState(0).

steps.title: Define increment handler
steps.instruction: Inside the useCounter hook, define a function named increment that increases the count state by 1.
steps.hint: Create a function that calls setCount with the current count plus 1.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useCounter hook now contains an increment function that will update the count state.
successCriteria: An increment function is defined inside useCounter that calls setCount with count + 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're defining a function named increment that updates the count state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The increment handler isn't defined correctly. Check that you're creating a function that increases count by 1.

steps.title: Type the custom hook return value as a tuple
steps.instruction: Add an explicit return type annotation to your useCounter hook: a tuple type [number, () => void, () => void].
steps.hint: Place the type annotation after the function name and parameters, before the opening brace: function useCounter(): [number, () => void, () => void] { ... }
steps.expectedOutcome: The useCounter hook now has an explicit TypeScript return type annotation specifying it returns a tuple of three elements: a number and two void functions.
successCriteria: The useCounter function declaration includes the return type annotation [number, () => void, () => void].
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added the exact tuple type annotation [number, () => void, () => void] after the function name and before the opening brace.
steps.feedbackWrong: The hook doesn't have the required tuple return type. Add : [number, () => void, () => void] after the function name to explicitly type the return value.

steps.title: Return the tuple from the custom hook
steps.instruction: Inside the useCounter hook, return the tuple [count, increment, decrement].
steps.hint: The return statement should come after all hook logic and handlers are defined.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useCounter hook now returns a tuple containing the count state and both handlers.
successCriteria: The useCounter hook returns an array with three elements: count, increment, and decrement.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're returning an array with exactly three elements: count, increment, and decrement.
steps.feedbackWrong: The hook should return an array containing the count state and both handler functions.

steps.title: Create main component
steps.instruction: Create a function component named App that will use the useCounter hook. The component should return a JSX element (like a div).
steps.hint: Define a function called App that returns JSX. You can start with a simple div for now.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a functional component named App that returns JSX.
successCriteria: The App component is defined as a function and returns a JSX element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've defined a function named App that returns JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component isn't defined correctly. Check that you've created a function named App that returns JSX.

steps.title: Use the custom hook in the component
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, call the useCounter hook and destructure the returned tuple into variables named count, increment, and decrement.
steps.hint: Call the hook and destructure the array it returns into three variables in the order they were returned.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have access to the count state and increment/decrement handlers from the custom hook.
successCriteria: useCounter is called inside App and its return value is destructured into count, increment, and decrement variables.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling useCounter and destructuring all three values (count, increment, decrement) from the returned tuple.
steps.feedbackWrong: The hook isn't being used correctly. Call useCounter inside App and destructure its return value into three variables.

steps.title: Render component with hook functionality
steps.instruction: Inside your App component's return statement, replace null with JSX that displays the current count value and includes two buttons wired to the increment and decrement handlers.
steps.hint: Use curly braces to embed the count value in JSX, and set the onClick prop of each button to call the appropriate handler function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component renders a paragraph showing the count value and two buttons that, when clicked, will update the count via the typed tuple handlers.
successCriteria: The App component returns JSX containing a paragraph with {count} and two buttons with onClick handlers calling increment and decrement.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're displaying the count value in a paragraph and both buttons have onClick handlers that call the increment and decrement functions.
steps.feedbackWrong: The JSX is missing or incorrect. Ensure you replace null with JSX that includes a paragraph showing the count and two buttons with onClick handlers.
